title: The Payback Test Most Dental Practices Skip Before They Sign for New Equipment
linkedin:
Every dental principal has sat through the same pitch: a new scanner, a new crown mill, a promise that patients will request it by name.

The clinical case is usually solid. The commercial case rarely gets tested before the finance agreement is signed.

Here is the insight that changes the maths. In practices running an associate model, a share of every extra dollar new equipment generates leaves the practice as commission before the principal ever sees it. A scanner that lifts an associate's production nicely might only lift the practice's actual margin by a fraction of that.

Which means the payback calculation most principals run in their head, at the chair level, is not the number that matters. The number that matters is the practice level return once commission splits and lab fees are stripped out.

The fix is not complicated. Before signing for the next piece of equipment, work backwards from the known, fixed monthly repayment and ask how much extra production is genuinely needed to cover it, using your own production report rather than the vendor's case study.

Practices that run this test consistently end up buying fewer machines that sit idle in the corner, and get a clearer read on which chair is actually carrying the practice's profit.

A note for dental practice owners across Brisbane, Queensland, New South Wales and Victoria.

Spring is when a lot of the new equipment pitches land, whether it is an intraoral scanner, a CBCT unit or a same day crown mill. The clinical case for these purchases is usually genuine. What often gets skipped is testing whether the purchase actually pays for itself before the finance agreement is signed.

The maths is more complicated than it looks, especially in practices with associates on a commission structure. A share of every extra dollar the new equipment generates leaves the practice as commission before the principal ever sees it, which means the return at the practice level is smaller than the return the equipment appears to generate at the chair.

A simple way to test any equipment decision is to work backwards from the actual monthly finance repayment and ask how much extra production is genuinely needed, using your own production numbers rather than a best case projection from the sales pitch.

Practices that run this test tend to buy fewer machines that end up sitting idle, and get a clearer picture of which chair is really carrying the practice's profit.

If you are weighing up a purchase this quarter, it is worth ten minutes with your own numbers first. Read the full piece on the ProfitPulse blog.
